sections.title: 1. Territorial Limits & Distribution of Legislative Subjects

masteryZone.q: Which of the following describes the distribution of residuary legislative powers under the Indian Constitution?
opts: Vested in State Legislatures
Vested in the Parliament of India
Divided equally between Centre and States
Vested in the President of India
masteryZone.sol: Under Article 248, residuary powers of legislation (subjects not in any list) are vested in the Parliament of India, following the Canadian model.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the territorial extent of laws? (Select all that apply)
opts: Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India.
Only Parliament has the power to make laws with extra-territorial operation.
State legislatures can make laws that apply outside their states without any conditions.
State laws can apply extra-territorially if there is a sufficient territorial nexus.
masteryZone.sol: Parliament has extra-territorial law-making powers. State legislatures can only apply laws extra-territorially if there is a valid 'territorial nexus' between the state and the subject matter.

masteryZone.q: True or False: If a subject is listed in the Concurrent List, both the Centre and the States can make laws on it, but the Concurrent List does not contain entries for taxation.
masteryZone.sol: True. To avoid conflict, tax entries are kept out of the Concurrent List (with the exception of GST under Article 246A).

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: Article ________ of the Constitution was inserted by the 101st Amendment Act to provide concurrent power on GST.
masteryZone.sol: Article 246A gives concurrent legislative power to both Centre and States regarding GST.

masteryZone.q: Match the Seventh Schedule Lists with their original subject counts:
masteryZone.sol: The original counts were: Union (97), State (66), Concurrent (47).

masteryZone.q: Which model of federation did India follow by vesting residuary powers in the Centre?
masteryZone.sol: The Canadian model.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): A state law on a concurrent subject that is repugnant to a central law is void to the extent of repugnancy.
Reason (R): Article 254 establishes the supremacy of central legislation over state legislation on concurrent matters.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are true. Article 254 (repugnancy rule) establishes central supremacy in concurrent matters, directly explaining why conflicting state laws become void.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976:
Statement I: It transferred five subjects, including education and forests, from the State List to the Concurrent List.
Statement II: It abolished the residuary powers of the Parliament.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because the 42nd Amendment did not abolish residuary powers; they remain with Parliament.

masteryZone.q: Why did the makers of the Indian Constitution vest residuary powers in the Centre instead of the States?
masteryZone.sol: To strengthen the central government and prevent centrifugal forces, ensuring national unity and stability during the country's formative years.

masteryZone.q: How does the 'Doctrine of Territorial Nexus' save a state law from being declared extra-territorial and void?
masteryZone.sol: By proving that a real, substantial, and non-illusory connection exists between the state enacting the law and the object/person/activity outside the state being affected by the law.

masteryZone.q: State A passes a lottery tax law. Company X, registered in State B, organizes lottery tickets sold in State A. Company X challenges State A's tax law on the grounds of extra-territoriality. Determine the validity of the tax.
masteryZone.sol: The tax is valid. Under the Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, since the lottery tickets are sold and profit is generated within State A, there is a sufficient connection (nexus) to justify State A taxing the out-of-state company.

masteryZone.q: Explain the three-fold distribution of legislative subjects in India and how conflicts of overlap are resolved.
masteryZone.sol: The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative subjects into three lists: Union List (exclusive Centre), State List (exclusive State), and Concurrent List (joint jurisdiction). Conflicts are resolved using the principle of Federal Supremacy: (1) Union List prevails over State and Concurrent Lists in case of overlap, (2) Concurrent List prevails over State List in case of overlap, and (3) Central laws prevail over state laws on Concurrent List conflicts (Article 254), unless the state law has received the President's assent.

sections.title: 2. Parliament's Intrusion into the State Field

masteryZone.q: Under Article 249, Parliament can legislate on a state subject only if the resolution is passed by the Rajya Sabha by:
opts: Simple majority of the House
Absolute majority of the House
Two-thirds of the members present and voting
Special majority under Article 368
masteryZone.sol: Article 249 requires a resolution passed by the Rajya Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

masteryZone.q: Under which of the following circumstances can Parliament make laws on matters listed in the State List? (Select all that apply)
opts: When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest (Art 249).
During the operation of a Proclamation of National Emergency (Art 250).
Upon a request made by two or more States (Art 252).
Whenever the Prime Minister issues an executive decree.
masteryZone.sol: Articles 249, 250, and 252 are constitutional exceptions enabling Parliament to legislate on state subjects. The Prime Minister has no such decree power.

masteryZone.q: True or False: A law made by Parliament under Article 253 to implement an international treaty requires the ratification of at least half of the state legislatures.
masteryZone.sol: False. Article 253 gives absolute power to Parliament to implement international treaties without needing any state ratification or consent.

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: Laws made by Parliament on state subjects during a National Emergency (Art 250) cease to have effect ________ months after the emergency Proclamation stops operating.
masteryZone.sol: Under Article 250(2), such laws expire six months after the emergency ceases to operate.

masteryZone.q: Match the Parliamentary intrusion article with its activating condition:

options.text: Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest
Legislatures of two or more states pass a requesting resolution

masteryZone.sol: Article 249 matches Rajya Sabha resolution; Article 252 matches request of states; Article 253 matches international treaties.

masteryZone.q: What is the maximum duration for which a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 remains active?
masteryZone.sol: One year (but it can be extended for further periods of one year at a time).

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): A law passed by Parliament under Article 252 can only be amended or repealed by Parliament, not by the states.
Reason (R): The requesting states surrender their legislative competence over that subject to Parliament by passing a resolution.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are true. Because the states surrender their law-making power on that subject under Article 252, only Parliament retains the competence to amend or repeal the resulting law.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding laws passed during President's Rule:
Statement I: Laws made by Parliament for a state during President's Rule automatically expire 6 months after the rule ends.
Statement II: The state legislature can alter or repeal these laws after President's Rule ceases.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Statement I is incorrect because these laws do not automatically expire. Statement II is correct: the state legislature has full power to amend or repeal them once normal state administration is restored.

masteryZone.q: Why does Article 253 allow Parliament to legislate on state subjects to implement treaties without state consent?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure that India can fulfill its international commitments uniformly, preventing individual states from blocking national foreign policy decisions.

masteryZone.q: How does the federal character of India change during a National Emergency in terms of legislative powers?
masteryZone.sol: It temporarily converts into a unitary system where the legislative division of powers is suspended, and Parliament gains concurrent power to make laws on any subject in the State List for the entire country.

masteryZone.q: The Government of India signs an international convention on biodiversity. Parliament passes a law regulating agricultural land use (a state subject) to comply with the convention. State X challenges the law as an infringement of state autonomy. Evaluate the legal outcome.
masteryZone.sol: Parliament's law is constitutional. Under Article 253, Parliament has absolute power to legislate on any state subject to implement international treaties or agreements, and this power overrides the standard distribution of subjects in the Seventh Schedule.

masteryZone.q: Explain the five constitutional provisions that enable Parliament to legislate on subjects in the State List.
masteryZone.sol: Parliament can legislate on state subjects under: (1) Article 249: when Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3 majority in the national interest, (2) Article 250: during a National Emergency, (3) Article 252: when two or more states request Parliament to make a law, (4) Article 253: to implement international treaties and conventions, and (5) Article 356: during President's Rule in a state.

sections.title: 3. Centre's Control over State Legislation & Judicial Principles

masteryZone.q: When a Governor reserves a state bill for the consideration of the President, the President is:
opts: Bound to give assent within 3 months
Bound to return the bill if it is passed again by the state
Under no constitutional time limit and can withhold assent indefinitely
Bound to refer it to the Supreme Court
masteryZone.sol: The President is under no time limit and enjoys absolute veto power over state bills reserved under Article 201.

masteryZone.q: Under which of the following conditions must state bills be reserved or sanctioned by the President? (Select all that apply)
opts: Bills imposing trade restrictions between states (Art 304(b)).
Bills derogating the power of the High Court (mandatory Governor reservation).
Money bills during a Financial Emergency (Art 360).
All ordinary bills passed by a state legislature.
masteryZone.sol: Trade restriction bills, High Court power derogation bills, and money/financial bills during financial emergencies require President's involvement. Standard ordinary bills do not.

masteryZone.q: True or False: The 'Doctrine of Colorable Legislation' is used to test the intentions or motives of the legislature when enacting a law.
masteryZone.sol: False. The doctrine is concerned with the legislative competence (power) of the legislature, not its motives or intentions. 'Colorable' means the legislature has disguised its lack of power.

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: The Doctrine of ________ is applied when courts look at the 'true nature and character' of a law to resolve list overlaps.
masteryZone.sol: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance examines the core matter of a law to determine which list it belongs to.

masteryZone.q: Match the judicial doctrine with its core constitutional maxim:

options.text: True nature and character of the law
What cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly
Sufficient connection between state and subject

masteryZone.sol: Pith and Substance matches true nature; Colorable Legislation matches indirect actions; Territorial Nexus matches sufficient connection.

masteryZone.q: Which article of the Constitution governs the reservation of bills by the Governor for the President?
masteryZone.sol: Article 200 (Article 201 details the President's actions on reserved bills).

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The President has absolute veto power over state bills reserved for his consideration.
Reason (R): The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit within which the President must declare his assent or veto.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are true. The lack of a time limit is the primary reason the President can withhold assent indefinitely, establishing an absolute veto.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding central control over state laws:
Statement I: The Governor must reserve any state bill that endangers the constitutional position of the High Court.
Statement II: During a Financial Emergency, the Centre can demand all state money bills be reserved for the President.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct. High Court derogation is a mandatory reservation under Article 200, and money bill reservation is enabled under Article 360 during financial emergencies.

masteryZone.q: Why does the Constitution provide the President with veto power over state legislation?
masteryZone.sol: To protect national interest, ensure uniformity of laws on concurrent subjects, and prevent state legislatures from enacting laws that violate the Constitution or federal harmony.

masteryZone.q: How do courts apply the 'Doctrine of Pith and Substance' to save an overlapping law?
masteryZone.sol: By analyzing the law's main object, scope, and effect. If the core (pith) falls within the enacting body's list, the law is held valid, and any minor, incidental encroachment on another list is ignored.

masteryZone.q: A state assembly enacts a law on money lending (a state subject) but includes provisions regulating promissory notes (a Union subject). A borrower challenges the law as unconstitutional. Determine the validity of the law.
masteryZone.sol: The law is valid. Applying the Doctrine of Pith and Substance, the core subject is money lending (State List), and the regulation of promissory notes is merely an incidental encroachment necessary to make the state law effective.

masteryZone.q: Explain the judicial doctrines of 'Colorable Legislation' and 'Territorial Nexus' in Indian federalism.
masteryZone.sol: The Doctrine of Colorable Legislation prevents a legislature from bypassing its constitutional limits by pretending a law is within its powers when it is actually an indirect trespass into an unauthorized field. The Doctrine of Territorial Nexus ensures that state laws operate only within state boundaries, unless a clear, real, and sufficient connection exists between the state and the out-of-state subject matter, justifying extra-territorial application.
